title: Bollywood's Most Powerful Workers' Federation Just Banned Ranveer Singh. The Don 3 Dispute Has Gone From Creative Differences to an Industry Reckoning.
excerpt: FWICE issued a formal Non-Cooperation Directive after Ranveer ignored three notices over six weeks. Excel Entertainment claims ₹45 crore in pre-production losses. Ranveer says it's a legal matter, not a union one. Here's what NRIs need to understand about why this matters.
body:
The Federation of Western India Cine Employees — the body that represents everyone from camera operators to set designers across Bollywood — has formally banned Ranveer Singh. The Non-Cooperation Directive means no FWICE member is supposed to work with him until the matter is resolved.

This is no longer a gossip-column disagreement. It's a formal industry action against one of Bollywood's biggest stars, triggered by his exit from *Don 3* and his refusal to engage with the federation that governs the industry he works in.

## How It Escalated

The timeline is important.

Farhan Akhtar filed a formal complaint with IFTDA (the directors' association) on April 11, 2026. The complaint was referred to FWICE. Over the next six weeks, FWICE sent Ranveer three notices — on April 22, April 30, and May 13 — inviting him to appear and present his side.

Ranveer didn't respond to any of them. According to FWICE Chief Advisor Ashoke Pandit, the actor only engaged after FWICE announced it would address the matter publicly. And when he did respond, it wasn't to appear — it was to argue that FWICE "would not be the appropriate forum" and that the dispute was "contractual in nature" requiring "adjudication before the appropriate legal forum."

In other words: Ranveer's position is that this is a legal matter between him and Excel Entertainment, not a union grievance. FWICE's position is that an actor walking out of a committed project three weeks before shooting — after ₹45 crore in pre-production spending — is exactly the kind of issue a workers' federation exists to address.

## The Money

The numbers are staggering. Excel Entertainment, the production house co-founded by Farhan Akhtar and Ritesh Sidhwani, claims it invested approximately ₹45 crore in pre-production for *Don 3* based on Ranveer's commitment to the project. That includes location scouting, set construction, costume design, crew contracts, and Farhan Akhtar's own schedule — which he blocked specifically for this film.

For context, ₹45 crore is more than the entire budget of many successful Hindi films. It's more than *12th Fail* cost to make. It's nearly the budget of *Stree 2*. The idea that this amount was spent before a single frame was shot — and that the lead actor then walked away — is what makes this dispute unusual even by Bollywood's standards.

Reports suggest Ranveer has agreed to return his ₹10 crore signing fee. But that still leaves a gap of ₹35 crore that Excel is seeking to recover.

## The Creative Split

The industry consensus, based on multiple reports, is that the disagreement was creative. Ranveer reportedly pushed for a darker, more aggressive interpretation of the Don character — understandable given his recent transformation into one of Bollywood's most physical performers after *Dhurandhar*. The production team wanted to maintain the franchise's established style: slick, glamorous, Shah Rukh Khan's swagger in a new body.

After *Dhurandhar* made him the lead of Bollywood's biggest-ever hit (₹1,184 crore in India), Ranveer's leverage changed. The actor who signed on for *Don 3* was not the same actor who emerged from *Dhurandhar*'s stratospheric success. His sense of what he could demand — creatively and commercially — had shifted.

## Why This Matters Beyond Bollywood

For NRIs, the FWICE ban might seem like inside-baseball — an industry dispute that doesn't affect whether you watch Ranveer's next film. But there are larger implications.

First, the Don franchise is deeply personal for diaspora audiences. Shah Rukh Khan's *Don* was a defining film for a generation of NRIs. Ranveer inheriting that role was already controversial. His walking away from it — and the ugly fallout — adds another layer to the franchise's complicated legacy.

Second, this is about the economics of star power in modern Bollywood. When a single actor can cause ₹45 crore in losses by changing their mind, it raises questions about how the industry manages risk. Hollywood has completion bonds and insurance for exactly this scenario. Bollywood, which operates largely on personal relationships and verbal commitments, doesn't.

Third, the FWICE directive has teeth — in theory. If enforced, no camera operator, gaffer, stylist, or assistant director affiliated with FWICE would be able to work on a Ranveer Singh project. In practice, these bans are rarely permanent. They're pressure tactics designed to bring the parties to the table.

## What Happens Next

Ranveer's spokesperson has released a measured statement emphasising "dignity, maturity, and mutual respect" — the diplomatic language of someone who knows this will eventually be settled privately. The Producers Guild of India is reportedly mediating.

Don 3, meanwhile, is in limbo. Farhan Akhtar is said to be exploring his options — but with Ranveer out and no replacement announced, the film's future is uncertain.

For Ranveer, the immediate impact is reputational rather than practical. He has other projects lined up. But the image of Bollywood's biggest star being formally banned by the industry's largest workers' body is not one that fades quickly — especially when the amount in dispute could finance an entire film.

Ranveer's exit — and now a formal industry ban — raises questions about how Bollywood handles star power in an era of ₹1,000+ crore blockbusters. The ₹45 crore dispute amount exceeds the total budget of most mid-tier Hindi films.
